title: Ordinary Annuity and Annuity Due (Find Future Value)

discoveryHook.scenario: A lottery winner receives $1 million, but not as a lump sum. Instead, the state makes annual payments of $50,000 for 20 years. That stream of equal payments is an [[kw:annuity]]. An annuity can be ordinary (payments at end of period) or annuity due (payments at beginning).

blocks.title: 1. Concept of an Annuity

hints: Each deposit earns one extra period of compounding.
challengeCorner.prompt: If you deposit $1,000 at the beginning of each year for 4 years at 6%, will the future value be greater or less than if deposits were at year-end? (word: greater or less)

confusionCorner.body: Don't confuse annuity with a lump sum. [[imp:An annuity involves multiple equal payments; a lump sum is a single deposit.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

explanation: An [[kw:annuity]] is a series of equal payments made at regular intervals (monthly, quarterly, annually, etc.).
[[kw:Ordinary annuity]]: payments occur at the end of each period (e.g., mortgage payments, bond interest).
[[kw:Annuity due]]: payments occur at the beginning of each period (e.g., rent, insurance premiums).
[[kw:Future value of an annuity]] is the total amount accumulated at the end of the annuity term, including all payments plus compound interest.
[[imp:The last payment in an ordinary annuity earns no interest because it is deposited at the end of the final period.]]

visuals.title: Annuity Classifications
visuals.caption: The payment timing affects the future value: annuity due earns one extra period of interest.

notes: Each payment earns interest from its deposit date to the end of the annuity term.
Payments later in the schedule earn less interest.

blocks.title: 2. Ordinary Annuity: Manual Calculation

visuals.caption: Last payment earns no interest. Total interest = $739.20.
visuals.title: Manual Calculation: $3,000 at 8% for 3 years

explanation: Manual calculation for ordinary annuity:
1. At the end of year 1, the first payment is deposited; no interest earned yet.
2. At the end of year 2, last year's balance earns interest, then the second payment is added.
3. Repeat for each period.
The process: new balance = (old balance × (1 + i)) + new payment.
[[imp:Interest is calculated before adding the new payment, because the payment is made at the end of the period.]]

notes: First payment earns interest for (n–1) periods; last earns 0.
formulaCard.title: Ordinary Annuity – Manual Steps

teacherCues: Walk through the steps: after each period, add new deposit, then calculate interest.
Use the example of $3,000 deposited at end of each year for 3 years at 8%.

challengeCorner.prompt: Invest $1,500 at end of each year for 3 years at 10%. Compute FV manually.
hints: Each year, multiply previous balance by 1.10, then add $1,500.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Don't add the payment before calculating interest. [[imp:In an ordinary annuity, interest is computed on the balance before the payment is added.]]

discoveryHook.scenario: You invest $3,000 at the end of each year for 3 years at 8%. After year 1: $3,000 (no interest). After year 2: ($3,000 × 1.08) + $3,000 = $6,240. After year 3: ($6,240 × 1.08) + $3,000 = $9,739.20. The total invested was $9,000, but it grew to $9,739.20 — the extra $739.20 is compound interest.

steps: In an ordinary annuity, payments are at the end of the period.
The last payment is made at the very end of the term, so there is no remaining time for it to earn interest.
Thus it simply adds to the final balance without any growth.

confusionCorner.body: Make sure to use the ordinary annuity table, not the lump‑sum future value table. [[imp:Ordinary annuity factors are ≥ 1; lump‑sum factors are (1+i)^n.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

visuals.caption: Factor for $1 per period; multiply payment by factor to get FV.
visuals.title: Ordinary Annuity FV Table (Excerpt)

explanation: An [[kw:ordinary annuity future value table]] gives the future value of $1 per period for various i and n.
Steps: 1. Determine i and n. 2. Find the table factor. 3. Multiply the periodic payment by the factor.
$$FV = \text{Payment} \times \text{Table Factor}$$
The factor accounts for compound interest on all but the last payment.
[[imp:The table factor increases with both n and i.]]

formulaCard.title: FV of Ordinary Annuity by Table
notes: n = number of payments, i = periodic rate.
If the exact n or i is not in the table, use the formula or interpolation.

examples.title: A – Use table

Explain why using a table is more efficient than manual calculation for longer annuities.
examples.title: B – Table vs. manual
steps: Manual calculation requires one step per period.
The table condenses all that into a single factor and one multiplication.

examples.prompt: Quarterly deposits of $500 are made for 2 years at 3% per quarter. Table factor for n=8, i=3% is 8.8923. Find FV.
examples.title: C – Find FV from table

discoveryHook.scenario: Instead of manual calculations, we can use an [[kw:ordinary annuity future value table]]. For $1 deposited at end of each period, the table shows total future value. For $3,000 annually for 3 years at 8%, the factor is 3.2464. FV = $3,000 × 3.2464 = $9,739.20. One multiplication replaces all the manual steps.

teacherCues: Show an ordinary annuity future value table.
Explain that the table factor = sum of compounded values of $1 per period.

blocks.title: 4. Annuity Due: Payments at Beginning

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Don't use the annuity due formula if payments are at the end of the period. [[imp:Identify payment timing before choosing the method.]]

examples.title: A – Convert ordinary to due
examples.prompt: Ordinary annuity FV = $9,739.20, i = 8%. Find annuity due FV.

examples.peerPrompt: Think about shifting each payment one period earlier.
examples.title: B – Why multiply by (1+i)?
steps: In annuity due, each payment is made one period earlier than in an ordinary annuity.
Thus each payment earns interest for one extra period.
Multiplying the entire ordinary FV by (1+i) adds that extra period of compounding to the total.
examples.prompt: Explain why multiplying the ordinary FV by (1+i) gives the annuity due FV.
Ordinary FV = $2,050, i = 5%. Find annuity due FV.
examples.title: C – Find annuity due FV

teacherCues: Show that annuity due FV = Ordinary annuity FV × (1 + i).
Explain: each payment earns one extra period of interest.

discoveryHook.scenario: If the same $3,000 payments were made at the beginning of each year instead of the end, the future value would be higher. For annuity due, each deposit earns interest for one extra period. FV due = FV ordinary × (1 + i). At 8%, FV due = $9,739.20 × 1.08 = $10,518.34.

visuals.title: Ordinary vs. Annuity Due FV ($3,000, 8%, 3 years)
visuals.caption: Annuity due FV = ordinary FV × 1.08.

explanation: [[kw:Annuity due]]: payments are made at the beginning of each period.
The first payment earns interest for all n periods, the second for n–1, etc.
To compute FV of annuity due from ordinary FV: $$FV_{\text{due}} = FV_{\text{ordinary}} \times (1 + i)$$.
Alternatively, use an annuity due table (factor = ordinary factor × (1+i)).
[[imp:For the same payment, rate, and n, annuity due always yields a higher FV than ordinary annuity.]]

formulaCard.title: Annuity Due FV from Ordinary FV
notes: This assumes you already have the ordinary FV from manual or table.
Alternatively, use an annuity due table factor.

formulaCard.title: Annuity Blueprint Formulas
notes: Always compute n and i first.
Check payment timing (end or beginning) before choosing formula.

explanation: Apply the blueprint to annuity problems:
1. Understand: identify payment amount, frequency, annual rate, payment timing (end or beginning), and number of years.
2. Solve: determine n and i; choose ordinary or annuity due table/factor; compute FV = Payment × Factor (and adjust for annuity due if needed).
3. Conclude: state the future value; verify that total payments plus interest meets the goal.
This organizes the information and prevents timing errors.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: If the problem does not state whether payments are at beginning or end, assume end of period (ordinary annuity). [[imp:Explicitly clarify timing before solving.]]
